title: Genomic Editing in Human NK Cells via CRISPR-Cas9 Ribonucleoproteins
author: Verhezen, Lau, et al.

Investigating both genetic and protein levels is important for comprehensive characterization of edited NK cells. While genetic analysis provides insights into the underlying genomic alterations induced by gene editing, protein-level assessment offers a measure of functional changes at the cellular level. To assess the edited NK cells on protein level, flow cytometry was used. Here, we explain how to stain for both intracellular and extracellular proteins. Representative results are shown below. Samples were acquired on the NovoCyte Quanteon Flow Cytometer System and analyzed using FlowJo (TreeStar). steps.title: Select nucleofection cuvette or strip
steps.instruction: Choose Lonza 4D Nucleofector cuvettes or strips according to the desired cell quantity; the protocol provides optimized sgRNA‑Cas9 ratios and nucleofection programs for resting primary human NK cells and NK‑92 cells.

steps.title: Select sgRNAs and design primers
steps.instruction: Pick three distinct sgRNAs targeting the same genomic region and design PCR primers to amplify the target locus; annotate gene, sgRNAs and primers using software such as CLC Workbench (Qiagen) or SnapGene (Dotmatics).

steps.title: Isolate PBMCs from buffy coats
steps.instruction: Perform density‑gradient isolation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from healthy donor buffy coats.

substeps.instruction: 1. Disinfect the blood bag and tube; cut the tube and release ~40 mL blood into a 50 mL Falcon tube.
2. Fill two 50 mL tubes with 15 mL Ficoll‑Paque or LymphoPrep (density gradient medium).
3. Carefully layer the blood onto the gradient medium (≈20 mL per tube) without mixing.
4. Centrifuge 10 min at 890 × g, maximal acceleration, with rotor brakes off.
5. Collect the buffy‑coat layer from each tube and transfer to separate 50 mL Falcon tubes; add 40 mL PBS‑EDTA and resuspend.
6. Centrifuge 10 min at 450 × g; discard supernatant containing platelets.
7. Resuspend pellet 1 in 25 mL 1× red blood cell lysis buffer and transfer to the second tube; also resuspend pellet 2 in the same buffer, ending with one tube containing all PBMCs.
8. Add DNase‑1 to 50 U/mL, rotate gently for 1 min to prevent clotting.
9. Centrifuge 5 min at 450 × g; discard supernatant with lysed red cells.
10. Resuspend cells in 50 mL PBS‑EDTA.
11. Filter through a 70 µm cell strainer.
12. Count cells with an automated counter using trypan blue; expect 90 %–99 % viability.
13. OPTIONAL pause: keep PBMCs overnight at 1–1.6 × 10⁷ cells/mL in RPMI + supplements at 37 °C; add 50 U/mL DNase‑1.

steps.title: Isolate primary NK cells
steps.instruction: Enrich resting NK cells from PBMCs by negative selection using Biotin‑Antibody cocktail, Streptavidin NanoBeads and magnetic columns (BioLegend MoJo Sort).

substeps.instruction: 1. Determine number of columns needed (max 1 × 10⁸ PBMC per column).
2. Transfer appropriate PBMC volume to a 50 mL tube.
3. Centrifuge 5 min at 300 × g; discard supernatant.
4. Resuspend cells in 100 µL MACS buffer per 10⁷ cells.
5. Dilute NK Cell Biotin‑Antibody Cocktail 1:4 in MACS buffer; add 10 µL per 10⁷ cells.
6. Incubate on ice 15 min.
7. Add 4 mL MACS buffer, centrifuge 5 min at 300 × g; discard supernatant.
8. Resuspend pellet in 100 µL MACS buffer per 10⁷ cells.
9. Dilute NK Cell Streptavidin NanoBeads 1:4 in MACS buffer; add 10 µL per 10⁷ cells.
10. Incubate on ice 15 min.
11. Add 4 mL MACS buffer, centrifuge 5 min at 300 × g; discard supernatant.
12. Resuspend pellet in 3 mL MACS buffer per column; keep on ice.
13. Place 15 mL Falcon tubes beneath each column to collect flow‑through (unlabeled NK cells).
14. Pre‑wash each column with 3 mL MACS buffer.
15. Load 3 mL cell suspension per column, avoiding bubbles and dryness.
16. Wash each column 2–3 times with 3 mL MACS buffer.
17. After final wash, centrifuge NK cells, discard supernatant, and resuspend in primary NK cell medium; pool all columns.
18. Assess purity by flow cytometry:
a. Add 1 × 10⁵ PBMC and 1 × 10⁵ NK cells to separate polystyrene FACS tubes.
b. Wash with 2 mL FACS buffer, centrifuge 5 min at 450 × g (19 °C–22 °C), discard supernatant.
c. Resuspend pellets in 100 µL FACS buffer; add 5 µL anti‑CD3 FITC and 5 µL anti‑CD56 PE.
d. Incubate 15 min at room temperature (19 °C–22 °C) in the dark.
e. Wash with 2 mL FACS buffer, centrifuge 5 min at 450 × g (19 °C–22 °C), discard supernatant.
f. Resuspend in 100 µL FACS buffer and acquire on a flow cytometer.
g. Expect >90 % CD3⁻CD56⁺ NK cells.
19. Count NK cells; either proceed directly to CRISPR editing or keep overnight.
20. NOTE: For activated NK cells, cytokine pre‑stimulation may be required and nucleofection pulse codes may need re‑optimization.

steps.title: Culture NK‑92 cells
steps.instruction: Maintain NK‑92 cell line and activate 24 h before nucleofection.

substeps.instruction: 1. Grow NK‑92 in α‑MEM supplemented with 12.5 % FBS, 12.5 % horse serum, 2 mM L‑glutamine, 1 % pen‑strep, and 100 U/mL recombinant human IL‑2 at 0.25–0.4 × 10⁶ cells/mL.
2. Passage every 3–4 days.
3. One day before nucleofection, adjust density to 1 × 10⁶ cells/mL and add IL‑2 at the same concentration as in routine culture.

steps.title: Count and wash NK cells
steps.instruction: Prepare primary or NK‑92 cells for nucleofection by counting and washing.

substeps.instruction: 1. Count freshly isolated primary NK cells or overnight‑activated NK‑92 cells.
2. Transfer the desired number to an RNase‑free sterile Eppendorf tube (1–2 × 10⁶ cells for strips; 3–5 × 10⁶ cells for cuvettes).
3. Centrifuge 5 min at 200 × g; discard culture medium.
4. Wash cells with 1 mL PBS; centrifuge 5 min at 200 × g and discard PBS.

steps.title: Genomic editing analysis via Sanger sequencing
steps.instruction: Extract genomic DNA from edited NK cells, amplify the target region, and prepare PCR products for sequencing.

substeps.instruction: 1. Two to three days post‑nucleofection, count cells and split as needed.
2. Pellet 5 × 10⁵ cells; store dry pellets at –80 °C (up to 6 months) if not proceeding immediately.
3. Add 50 µL QuickExtract (QE) DNA Extraction Solution to the pellet, pulse‑vortex 30 s, and transfer to PCR tubes.
4. Run the following QE thermocycler program: 65 °C 15 min → 98 °C 10 min → hold 4 °C.
5. Measure genomic DNA concentration with Nanodrop or Qubit, using QE solution as blank.
6. Prepare PCR master mix per reaction (total 25 µL): 0.5 µL DNA polymerase (1 U/µL), 0.75 µL forward primer (10 µM), 0.75 µL reverse primer (10 µM), 5 µL 5× high‑fidelity buffer, ddH₂O up to 25 µL.
7. Aliquot 20–24 µL master mix to each tube (volume depends on DNA amount).
8. Add 10–100 ng genomic DNA (≤5 µL) to each tube; final volume 25 µL.

9. PCR cycling (KAPA HiFi HotStart recommended): Initial denaturation 95 °C 3 min; 25–35 cycles of 98 °C 20 s, annealing 60 °C–75 °C (primer‑specific, determine via gradient), extension 72 °C 15 s; final extension 72 °C 1 min; hold 4 °C.
10. Verify PCR product on agarose gel electrophoresis.
11. Quantify PCR product DNA (Qubit/Nanodrop) to ensure suitable concentration for sequencing.
12. Purify PCR amplicon using a method of choice (e.g., Promega Wizard SV PCR Clean‑Up kit).

steps.title: Sanger sequencing and ICE analysis
steps.instruction: Submit purified amplicons for Sanger sequencing and analyze indel frequencies with ICE.

substeps.instruction: 1. Send both forward‑ and reverse‑primer amplicons of each sample (edited and non‑edited control) to a sequencing provider.
2. In the ICE web tool, label each sample, paste the sgRNA sequences, leave the donor field blank, and upload the .ab1 files for control and edited samples.
3. Run the analysis to obtain indel percentages, knockout scores, and R² values.

steps.title: Intracellular protein staining for flow cytometry
steps.instruction: Fix, permeabilize, and stain intracellular proteins in edited NK cells for flow cytometric analysis.

substeps.instruction: 1. Transfer 2 × 10⁵ electroporated cells and 2 × 10⁵ unedited cells to separate polystyrene FACS tubes.
2. Centrifuge 5 min at 450 × g (19 °C–22 °C) after adding 2 mL PBS‑EDTA; discard supernatant.
3. Resuspend pellets in 100 µL FACS buffer; add fixable live/dead stain (1 µL) and incubate 15 min at 19 °C–22 °C in the dark.
4. Wash with 2 mL PBS‑EDTA, centrifuge 5 min at 450 × g (19 °C–22 °C), discard supernatant.
5. Prepare 1:4 Fix/Perm buffer (1 part concentrate + 3 parts diluent).
6. Add 100 µL Fix/Perm buffer to each sample, vortex, and incubate 30 min at 19 °C–22 °C in the dark.
7. Centrifuge 5 min at 600 × g (19 °C–22 °C); discard supernatant.
8. Dilute 10X Permeabilization solution 1:10 with distilled water; add 200 µL 1X Permeabilization to each sample.
9. Centrifuge 5 min at 600 × g (19 °C–22 °C); discard supernatant.
10. Resuspend pellets in 100 µL 1X permeabilization buffer.
11. Block with 2 % human serum by adding 2 µL directly to cells; incubate 15 min at 19 °C–22 °C.
12. Without washing, add the recommended volume of fluorochrome‑conjugated intracellular antibody; incubate 45 min at 19 °C–22 °C protected from light.
13. Add 200 µL 1X permeabilization buffer, centrifuge 5 min at 600 × g (19 °C–22 °C), discard supernatant.
14. Resuspend stained cells in appropriate volume of FACS buffer and acquire on a flow cytometer.

steps.title: Surface protein staining for flow cytometry
steps.instruction: Stain membrane‑expressed proteins on edited and control NK cells.

substeps.instruction: 1. Transfer 1 × 10⁵ electroporated cells and 1 × 10⁵ unedited cells to separate polystyrene FACS tubes.
2. Add 2 mL FACS buffer, centrifuge 5 min at 450 × g (19 °C–22 °C), discard supernatant.
3. Resuspend pellets in 100 µL FACS buffer; add 1 µL fixable live/dead stain and 5 µL antibody of choice.
4. Incubate 15 min at 19 °C–22 °C in the dark.
5. Wash with 2 mL FACS buffer, centrifuge 5 min at 450 × g (19 °C–22 °C), discard supernatant.
6. Acquire samples on a flow cytometer.

description: The CRISPR-Cas9 system has revolutionized the field of molecular biology as a versatile genome-editing tool with a broad range of applications, including exciting possibilities for medical advancements in the field of cellular therapies. Guided by a short RNA molecule, Cas9 is targeted to a genomic locus and creates a DNA double-strand break. When the targeted locus is repaired by the non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) pathway, this error-prone repair mechanism re-ligates the double-strand breaks, introducing small insertions or deletions (indels) at the breakpoint. Indels within a coding exon of the gene can lead to frameshift mutations and premature stop codons, resulting in a knockout of the gene. This protocol represents a reliable and reproducible CRISPR-Cas9 method for precise genome editing in resting primary NK cells and NK-92 cells. Genetic engineering of human NK cells via stable delivery systems of Cas9, such as viral vectors, presents important constraints. Lentiviral and retroviral transduction, for instance, induces NK cell apoptosis and yields only a restricted number of edited cells.1,2,3 Concurrently, the sustained expression of Cas9 increases the potential for off-target genomic modifications.4 Considering these limitations, we have chosen to employ ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complex delivery via Nucleofection. RNP complexes consist of (multiple) synthetic guide (sg)RNA(s) and preformed Cas9 protein. Unlike the traditional crRNA:tracrRNA system, sgRNA requires no annealing step, as it is already a single piece RNA molecule that performs well for CRISPR-Cas9 applications. The retention of the Cas9 enzyme within the cells for a span of approximately 24 h provides an adequate time frame for effective cellular edits while minimizing off-target interactions. Our protocol employs a novel multi-guide approach with three distinct sgRNAs for efficient gene knockout in primary NK cells and the NK-92 cell line.
